cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Change What the Apology Is For
cards.instruction: Get an apology, then reveal that the original offense was only the first layer of what needs repair.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I accept your apology for breaking my vase. Now tell me when you knew the dog hadn't done it.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Straight away. I'll buy you another vase.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Keep your money. You watched me shut the dog out of this room for three days. That is the part you're going to put right.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I was embarrassed to admit it. Shall I let him back in?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Yes. Call him in. Then apologise to me for leaving me to punish him. Your embarrassment stopped you speaking; mine began when I found out who I'd believed.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 accepts one apology and demands knowledge account; A3 refuses money and orders repair of concealed blame; A5 grants B proposed access repair then specifies a deeper apology.

responseLogic.evidence: A3 uses B2 immediate knowledge to show knowing silence; A5 uses B4 offered entry and embarrassment explanation without introducing a new punishment.

relationship.evidence: B2 offers payment and B4 offers to let dog back in, both plausible attempts at repair that A redirects.

heightening.evidence: A5 accepts B4 practical solution but names A shame at having punished the dog, a deeper layer caused by the same silence.

specificity.evidence: A1 vase, A3 three-day exclusion and A5 return remain coherent; removed bed no longer requires invented confiscation.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 two emotional consequences are explicit; slightly long but earned by B4 embarrassment explanation.
